questions.problem:
$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}=2.1x(1-0.025x)-1.1xy \\ {y}^{′}=-5.5y+2xy\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the modified Lotka-Volterra model, where $x=x(t)$ represents the prey and $y=y(t)$ represents the predators. Find the maximum carrying capacity for the prey in the case of the complete absence of predators.

The maximum carrying capacity is
{{field-1}}.
questions.worked_solution:
The Lotka-Volterra predator-prey model with carrying capacity is given by

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}=ax(1-hx)-bxy \\ {y}^{′}=-cy+dxy\end{aligned}
$$

where $a,b,c,d,h$ are positive real constants. Here, $x=x(t)$ represents the prey and $y=y(t)$ represents the predators.

In our case, the equation describing the dynamics of the prey is given by

$$
{x}^{′}=2.1x(1-0.025x)-1.1xy
$$

where 

- the $2.1x(1-0.025x)$ term defines the growth, and

- the $-1.1xy$ term defines the decay due to interaction with predators.

In the case of the complete absence of predators, we have $y=0,$ and this equation becomes

$$
{x}^{′}=2.1x(1-0.025x).
$$

General solutions to this equation are logistic functions with two horizontal asymptotes defined by the equilibrium solutions, which can be found by solving the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}2.1x(1-0.025x)=0\,⇒\,x=0,\,40\end{aligned}
$$

So, the equilibria are $x=0$ and $x=40.$ The nonzero equilibrium gives the maximum capacity.

Therefore, the maximum carrying capacity for the prey in the case of the complete absence of predators is $40.$

questions.problem:
$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}=3x(1-0.2x)-xy \\ {y}^{′}=-3y+xy\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the Lotka-Volterra model with carrying capacity above, where $x=x(t)$ represents the prey and $y=y(t)$ represents the predators. The equilibria of the model are the following:

$(0,0),\,(${{field-1}}$,0),\,(${{field-2}}$,${{field-3}}$)$
questions.worked_solution:
The equilibrium (fixed) points of a system ${x}^{′}(t)=f(x,y)$ are the points for which $f(x,y)=0.$ So, we get the following system of linear equations:

$$
{\begin{aligned}3x(1-0.2x)-xy=0 \\ -3y+xy=0\end{aligned}
$$

Factoring the second equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}-3y+xy & =0 \\ y(-3+x) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, $y=0$ or $x=3.$ We consider both cases separately.

- If $y=0,$ substituting it into the first equation, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}3x(1-0.2x)-x(0) & =0 \\ 3x(0.2x-1) & =0 \\ x & =0,\,5.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the first two equilibria are $(0,0)$ and $(5,0).$

- If $x=3,$ substituting it into the first equation, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}3(3)(1-0.2(3))-(3)y & =0 \\ 3.6-3y & =0 \\ y & =1.2.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, another equilibrium is $(3,1.2).$

Therefore, the equilibria of the model are

$$
(0,0),\,(5,0),\,(3,1.2).
$$

questions.problem:
$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}=3x(1-0.3x)-4xy \\ {y}^{′}=-y+xy\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the Lotka-Volterra model with carrying capacity above, where $x=x(t)$ represents the prey and $y=y(t)$ represents the predators. Select the correct options in the reasoning below.$\,$ Evaluating the Jacobian of the system at the equilibrium ${x}^{∗}=[0,\,0]^{T},$ we get

| $J({x}^{∗})=\,\,$ |  | {{field-1}} | {{field-2}} |  | $\,.$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | {{field-3}} | {{field-4}} |  |  |  |

$\,$ The eigenvalues of the Jacobian matrix are 
{{field-5}}.

$\,$ Therefore, the equilibrium at ${x}^{∗}$ is 
{{field-6}}{{field-7}}.
questions.worked_solution:
Let's denote ${f}_{1}(x,y)=3x(1-0.3x)-4xy$ and ${f}_{2}(x,y)=-y+xy.$

Now, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(3x(1-0.3x)-4xy)=3-1.8x-4y,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(3x(1-0.3x)-4xy)=-4x \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(-y+xy)=y,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(-y+xy)=-1+x\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the Jacobian matrix is

$$
J=[\begin{aligned}3-1.8x-4y & -4x \\ y & -1+x\end{aligned}].
$$

Next, we evaluate the Jacobian at the equilibrium ${x}^{∗}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$ to get

$$
J({x}^{∗})=[\begin{aligned}3-1.8(0)-4(0) & -4(0) \\ 0 & -1+0\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}].
$$

The eigenvalues of the Jacobian matrix are ${\lambda }_{1}=3\text{ and }{\lambda }_{2}=-1.$ Since the eigenvalues are real with opposite signs, our equilibrium is $\text{an unstable}$ $\text{saddle}.$

questions.problem:
$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}=x(1-x)-xy \\ {y}^{′}=-y+2xy\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the Lotka-Volterra model with carrying capacity above, where $x=x(t)$ represents the prey and $y=y(t)$ represents the predators. Select the correct options in the reasoning below.$\,$ Evaluating the Jacobian of the system at the equilibrium ${x}^{∗}=[0.5,\,0.5]^{T},$ we get

| $J({x}^{∗})=\,\,$ |  | {{field-1}} | {{field-2}} |  | $\,.$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | {{field-3}} | {{field-4}} |  |  |  |

$\,$ The eigenvalues of the Jacobian matrix are 
{{field-5}}.

$\,$ Therefore, the equilibrium at ${x}^{∗}$ is 
{{field-6}}{{field-7}}.
questions.worked_solution:
Let's denote ${f}_{1}(x,y)=x(1-x)-xy$ and ${f}_{2}(x,y)=-y+2xy.$

Now, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x(1-x)-xy)=1-2x-y,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(x(1-x)-xy)=-x \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(-y+2xy)=2y,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(-y+2xy)=-1+2x\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the Jacobian matrix is

$$
J=[\begin{aligned}1-2x-y & -x \\ 2y & -1+2x\end{aligned}].
$$

Next, we evaluate the Jacobian at the equilibrium ${x}^{∗}=[\begin{aligned}0.5 \\ 0.5\end{aligned}]$ to get

$$
J({x}^{∗})=[\begin{aligned}1-2(0.5)-0.5 & -0.5 \\ 2(0.5) & -1+2(0.5)\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-0.5 & -0.5 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

To find the eigenvalues of the Jacobian matrix, we write down the characteristic equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}-0.5-\lambda  & -0.5 \\ 1 & -\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (-0.5-\lambda )(-\lambda )-1(-0.5) & =0 \\ \lambda (0.5+\lambda )+0.5 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}+0.5\lambda +0.5 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Solving the equation, we get the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1,2}=-0.25\pm 0.25\sqrt{7}\,\text{i}.$ Since the eigenvalues are complex with negative real parts, our equilibrium is $\text{an asymptotically stable}$ $\text{spiral sink}.$

\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(4x(1-2x)-xy)=4-16x-y,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(4x(1-2x)-xy)=-x \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(-3y+2xy)=2y,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(-3y+2xy)=-3+2x\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the Jacobian matrix is

$$
J=[\begin{aligned}4-16x-y & -x \\ 2y & -3+2x\end{aligned}].
$$

Next, we evaluate the Jacobian at the equilibrium ${x}^{∗}=[\begin{aligned}0.5 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$ to get

$$
J({x}^{∗})=[\begin{aligned}4-16(0.5)-0 & -0.5 \\ 2(0) & -3+2(0.5)\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-4 & -0.5 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}].
$$

The eigenvalues of the Jacobian matrix are ${\lambda }_{1}=-4\text{ and }{\lambda }_{2}=-2.$ Since the eigenvalues are real and both negative, our equilibrium is $\text{an asymptotically stable}$ $\text{sink}.$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Determining the Carrying Capacity for the Prey
canonical_examples.problem:
$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}=6x(1-0.1x)-3xy \\ {y}^{′}=-7y+5xy\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the modified Lotka-Volterra model, where $x=x(t)$ represents the prey and $y=y(t)$ represents the predators. Find the maximum carrying capacity for the prey in the case of the complete absence of predators.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The Lotka-Volterra predator-prey model with carrying capacity is given by

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}=ax(1-hx)-bxy \\ {y}^{′}=-cy+dxy\end{aligned}
$$

where $a,b,c,d,h$ are positive real constants. Here, $x=x(t)$ represents the prey and $y=y(t)$ represents the predators.

In our case, the equation describing the dynamics of the prey is given by

$$
x' = 6x(1-0.1x) - 3xy
$$

where 

- the $6x(1-0.1x)$ term defines the growth, and

- the $-3xy$ term defines the decay due to interaction with predators.

In the case of the complete absence of predators, we have $y = 0,$ and this equation becomes

$$
x' = 6x(1-0.1x).
$$

General solutions to this equation are logistic functions with two horizontal asymptotes defined by the equilibrium solutions, which can be found by solving the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}6x(1-0.1x)=0\,⇒\,x=0,\,10\end{aligned}
$$

So, the equilibria are $x=0$ and $x=10.$ The nonzero equilibrium gives the maximum capacity.

Therefore, the maximum carrying capacity for the prey in the case of the complete absence of predators is $10.$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Finding Equilibrium Points of the Modified Lotka-Volterra System
canonical_examples.problem:
$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}=5x(1-0.2x)-4xy \\ {y}^{′}=-6y+3xy\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the Lotka-Volterra model with carrying capacity above, where $x=x(t)$ represents the prey and $y=y(t)$ represents the predators. Find the equilibria of the model.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The equilibrium (fixed) points of a system $\mathbf{x}'(t) = \mathbf{f}(x,y)$ are the points for which $f(x,y)=\mathbf{0}.$ So, we get the following system of linear equations:

$$
{\begin{aligned}5x(1-0.2x)-4xy=0 \\ -6y+3xy=0\end{aligned}
$$

Factoring the second equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}-6y+3xy & =0 \\ y(-6+3x) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, $y=0$ or $x=2.$ We consider both cases separately.

- If $y=0,$ substituting it into the first equation, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}5x(1-0.2x)-4x(0) & =0 \\ 5x(0.2x-1) & =0 \\ x & =0,\,5.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the first two equilibria are $(0,0)$ and $(5,0).$

- If $x=2,$ substituting it into the first equation, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}5(2)(1-0.2(2))-(4)(2)y & =0 \\ 10(1-0.4)-8y & =0 \\ 10(0.6)-8y & =0 \\ 6-8y & =0 \\ y & =0.75.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, another equilibrium is $(2, 0.75).$

Therefore, the equilibria of the model are

$$
(0,0), \qquad
(5, 0), \qquad
(2, 0.75).
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Classifying Equilibria of the Modified Lotka-Volterra Model: Stable Case
canonical_examples.problem:
Consider the Lotka-Volterra model with carrying capacity below, where $x=x(t)$ represents the prey and $y=y(t)$ represents the predators.

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}=5x(1-x)-xy \\ {y}^{′}=-y+2xy\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluate the Jacobian of the system at the equilibrium point $\mathbf{x^\ast}=[0.5, \, 2.5]^T,$ and classify this equilibrium point.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Let's denote $f_1(x,y)=5x(1-x)-xy$ and $f_2(x,y)=-y+2xy.$

Now, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(5x(1-x)-xy)=5-10x-y,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(5x(1-x)-xy)=-x \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(-y+2xy)=2y,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(-y+2xy)=-1+2x\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the Jacobian matrix is
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14095078/assets/b046e51c9a1b68cc22e1bd46f532a8d8d70452e5549937aaa8d872e60c63eb20.png)

Next, we evaluate the Jacobian at the equilibrium ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14095078/assets/e91d26ba55bafc85ce58c65482858d3f2094136b9620fe5d6a30b514ffe59b87.png) to get

To find the eigenvalues of the Jacobian matrix, we write down the characteristic equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}-2.5-\lambda  & -0.5 \\ 5 & -\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (-2.5-\lambda )(-\lambda )-5(-0.5) & =0 \\ \lambda (2.5+\lambda )+2.5 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}+2.5\lambda +2.5 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Solving the equation, we get the eigenvalues $\lambda_{1,2} = -1.25 \pm 0.25\sqrt{15}\,\text{i}.$ Since the eigenvalues are complex with negative real parts, our equilibrium is an asymptotically stable spiral sink.
